did.abstract: The papers consist of correspondence with an international array of scholars, journalists, heads of state, government officials, and friends. Also included are manuscripts and drafts of his books, columns, and speeches. In addition there are diaries and engagement books, photographs of Walter Lippmann with family and friends, requests to speak or write, honors, and film and audio tapes.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: For almost seventy-five years of the twentieth century Walter Lippmann knew and corresponded with a great many men and women in most parts of the world who were deeply involved in and helped shape the course of events. His papers, starting in 1906 with his undergraduate years at Harvard and ending with his death in 1974 at the age of eighty-five, constitute an important contribution to the history of our own time. They give a picture of the public life of this century from the angle of vision of an author, editor, journalist and political philosopher. In the political drama, Walter Lippmann was back stage, on stage, and among the critics in the stalls.

The Walter Lippmann Papers (MS. Group No. 326), consisting of 115 linear feet of correspondence and other types of material, are divided into the following ten series: I. Correspondence, 1906-1930; II. Requests to Speak, Write or Reprint, 1906-1930; III. Correspondence, 1931-1981; IV. Requests To Speak, Write or Reprint, 1931-1974; V. Public Opinion Mail, 1935-1968; VI. Manuscripts and/or Typescripts, 1917-1967; VII. Diaries and Engagement Books, 1914-1974; VIII. Honors; IX. Photographs, Portraits, and Sketches, 1889-1979; X. Films, Recordings, and Tapes, 1914-1974.

Because of the volume of the papers, the first four series are divided into the periods 1906-1930 and 1931-1974. The year 1931 was considered a logical series break because Walter Lippmann's career as an editor ended with the demise of the New York World in February and his career as a columnist for the New York Herald Tribune began in September. A description of the content and arrangement of each of the ten series immediately precedes the folder listing for the series in this register.

Researchers should be aware that there are two Walter Lippmann manuscript groups at the Yale Library, with separate registers. The group described above, and in this register, is known as the Walter Lippmann Papers, Manuscript Group Number 326. The second is known as the Robert O. Anthony Collection of Walter Lippmann, 66. The distinction between the two is that Group 326 consists of Lippmann's personal papers and manuscripts of his writings, while Group 766 is, in general, a collection of his published work. Between the two collections, probably no other journalist and few public figures will have had a career so carefully and completely documented for the historian of the future.

Accession Note

The Walter Lippmann Papers (MS Group No. 326, Manuscripts and Archives) became the property of the Yale University Library by deed of gift in July 1944. Inasmuch as the 1940s were probably the busiest years of his career as author and columnist, Lippmann needed his files for reference purposes, and it was not until 1963, some twenty years later, that the papers were actually removed from his home in Washington, D.C., and deposited in the Yale Library.

As early as 1941 Walter Lippmann had given to Yale some 300 numbers of serials and pamphlets for the Yale War Collection through his long-time friend, Wilmarth S. Lewis, Yale '18, who was active in the affairs of the Yale Library. In 1942, Lippmann wrote his lawyer, Albert Stickney, that he had been asked by the Library of Congress and also by the Yale University Library to give them all his papers, and that this action would involve a change in his will when he knew more clearly just exactly what he wanted to do. Two years later, in a letter to Lewis dated July 3, 1944, Lippmann wrote: "I took the invitation from Yale as a favor to me, and a very great distinction, not as something I was doing for Yale. It never occurred to me to consult Harvard, where I had been an overseer, about my papers any more than I might have asked them if they were going to give me an honorary degree." Lewis replied on July 5th: "Needless to say, I am very happy that you have given Yale your papers. The Yale Library is one of the chief things in my life, and it is a joy for me to have this great collection. The scholars of the future will now have to come to Yale to study our time." On the same date, Charles Seymour, President of Yale University, wrote Lippmann: "May I express again and more titleatically our deep gratitude for the gift of your papers. Their value in the Yale collection will be obviously enormous," and in a letter the next day Lewis reminded Lippmann: "I first spoke to you about your papers two years ago."

The decision in 1944 also involved a collection of published works by and about Walter Lippmann which had been assembled as a hobby, beginning in 1931, by Robert Olney Anthony, Amherst '26, a telephone executive for the Bell System in New York City. His collection included magazine articles, a complete file of Lippmann's "Today and Tomorrow" column (1931-1967) which he indexed, other newspaper articles, bulletins and pamphlets concerning Lippmann, newspaper clippings, and books by, about, or prominently mentioning him. Both for the protection of the collection, and to increase its availability to scholars, it was a propitious time to transfer his collection to the Yale Library. Lippmann agreed that both collections should be kept together, and in 1944 when Lippmann decided to give his papers to Yale, Anthony also offered his associated collection. Two years later when Anthony was transferred from New York to the New England Telephone and Telegraph Company in Providence, Rhode Island, on December 2, 1946, his collection was transferred to the Yale Library. His collection is listed as the Robert O. Anthony Collection of Walter Lippmann (MS Group 766, Manuscripts and Archives). On December 3, 1946, Anthony was named curator of the newly-formed collection by the Yale Corporation.

During 1945 and early 1946 Lippmann sent to Yale several items, e.g., manuscripts of some of his books, and the announcement of his gift appeared in the press in June 1946. Also in 1946 at the time of the Anthony collection move, the library truck picked up Lippmann's bound volumes of the editorial pages of the New York World for the period 1924 through February 1931, which were in his office at the New York Herald Tribune in New York City.

It was not until February 1963, when he was almost seventy-four, that Lippmann felt he could give up the bulk of his papers, consisting at that time of forty-two large files of personal correspondence and two boxes of original manuscripts. They were shipped to Providence, Rhode Island, for processing by Anthony and eventual shipment to Yale. In 1964 another shipment arrived in Providence, consisting of diaries and engagement books through 1959.

In 1964, Richard H. Rovere began his work in both collections as the authorized biographer of Walter Lippmann, with the assistance of Gary Clarkson. Four years later, finding himself uneasy in the role of biographer without the assurance of complete independence as to content, Rovere, in 1968, found a successor in Ronald Steel, a journalist who had been a foreign service officer.

Accession 2001-M-077 originated with Lippmann's first wife, Faye, and presumably consists of materials left behind by Lippmann after their divorce. The addition provides a substantive supplement to the materials described above, particularly for Lippmann's undergraduate years at Harvard and for most of the 1910s. Included are his classroom notes and several academic papers from Harvard; correspondence with family, friends, and business associates; holograph and typescript drafts of many early writings, including his first three books; photographs; and personal papers. The papers in the accession provide documentation of Lippmann's early professional life.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Walter Lippmann was born in New York City on September 23, 1889. Following graduation from Harvard College in 1910, he began his career as a reporter, author, and political commentator. He served on the first editorial board of the New Republic and was secretary to The Inquiry, a group of experts assembled at the request of Woodrow Wilson to collect data in preparation for a peace conference following World War I. Lippmann was editor of the New York World from 1922-1931. In 1931, he began a column for the New York Herald Tribune , "Today and Tomorrow," which would later be syndicated nationally and which continued until 1967. Lippmann was the author of numerous books of political commentary and philosophy. He died on December 14, 1974 in New York City.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series I is divided into two sections: Selected Correspondence, 1906 - 1930 and General Correspondence, 1906 - 1930.

Selected Correspondence is arranged alphabetically by the name of the correspondent. Following the alphabetical listing are five boxes [boxes 36-40] of personal Lippmann materials, including correspondence with Harvard University, family correspondence, financial papers, and papers related to World War I, "The Inquiry," and the Paris Peace Conference.
General Correspondence is arranged chronologically by year. Within each year, letters are arranged alphabetically by correspondent.

The correspondence in this series begins in 1906 with Walter Lippmann's undergraduate days at Harvard. It continues through the founding in 1914 of the New Republic where he was one of the editors; his activity on "The Inquiry" which prepared data for the Paris Peace Conference; his service as a captain in World War I; and his work as a talent scout for Harcourt, Brace, and Company, with his first success in the publication in the United States of John Maynard Keynes' The Economic Consequences of the Peace in 1920. It concludes in 1930 with his career on the editorial staff of the New York World newspaper.

In 1917 and 1918 Lippmann served as secretary to a secret organization created by President Wilson, known as "The Inquiry," to prepare data for the Paris Peace Conference. This organization prepared eight of the Fourteen Points - points dealing with concrete territorial and political issues. It was not involved with the other six points dealing with freedom of the seas and the League of Nations. Material on "The Inquiry" in the Lippmann papers is sparse and incomplete, and the researcher on this subject is referred to the National Archives of the United States, "Records of the American Commission to Negotiate Peace." (Record Group 256).

Correspondence between Walter Lippmann and his first wife is practically non-existent, despite several efforts to locate it through Faye herself and her family. Born on March 23, 1893, Faye Albertson was the beautiful daughter of Ralph Albertson, an ordained minister in the Congregational Church. As an undergraduate, Walter Lippmann was one of the frequent visitors to "The Farm" on the banks of the Merrimac River in West Newbury, Massachusetts, home of the Albertson family. Walter Lippmann and Faye Albertson were married several years later, in 1917.

Lippmann had a highly developed sense of privacy and seldom wrote of his personal life to others, although he came close to doing this with Bernard Berenson. He also seemed to have a distaste for the past, not the historical data which delighted him, but his own past. Although not appearing dissatisfied with his professional career, or perhaps his private life, he focused on the present and the future which he could attempt to mold as he could not the past. It is significant that he used the title, "Today and Tomorrow," for his articles in the Metropolitan magazine 1915, and for his noted column in the New York Herald Tribune and the Washington Post from 1931 to 1967.

The researcher interested in the Lippmann family papers is directed to the separate "Lippmann" material at the end of the Selected Correspondence. Consisting of boxes 36-40, it also includes all correspondence related to Harvard University as well as papers dealing with Lippmann's financial affairs, his involvement in "The Inquiry," and his service in World War I.

Lippmann's correspondence concerning matters pertaining to the New Republic when he was one of the editors is filed under " New Republic" and is located in box 22, folders 875-878. Likewise, correspondence concerning the New York World during the 1920s is filed under " New York World" and is located in boxes 22, 23, and 24, folders 885-913. For the convenience of the researcher, the New York World Council Minutes from April 1924 through June 1927 have been filed separately under box 25, folders 914-920. The Council Minutes contain discussions held regularly by Ralph Pulitzer with his staff of Arthur Krock, Walter Lippmann, Herbert Bayard Swope, and others on policy and procedural matters.

It should be noted that Lippmann's correspondence with his publishers is filed under the name of the publishing house, for example, "Mitchell Kennerley Company," but correspondence with Mr. Kennerley on other matters is filed under "Kennerley, Mitchell," with a cross-reference to the company.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series II is divided into the following sections: Requests to Speak, Selected, 1906-1930; Requests to Speak, General, 1906-1930; Requests to Write, General, 1906-1930; Requests to Write, Selected, 1906-1930; Requests to Reprint, 1906-1930

Requests are arranged alphabetically by the name of the institution or group, except for Requests to Speak, General, which is arranged chronologically by year. Within each year, items are arranged alphabetically.

It should be noted that requests to speak from speakers' bureaus are filed under the name of the bureau, for example, "Alber Bureau," but correspondence with Mr. Alber on other matters is filed under "Alber, Louis J." in Series I, Correspondence, 1906-1930. Likewise, requests to write from publishing companies are filed under the name of the company, for example "Alfred A. Knopf, Inc.," but correspondence with Mr. Knopf on other matters is filed under "Knopf, Alfred A.," in Series I. In the same manner, requests for permission to reprint are filed under the name of the company, for example, "Simon and Schuster," but correspondence with Mr. Schuster on other matters is filed under "Schuster, M. Lincoln," in Series I.

Sheer volume dictated the decision to separate from his other correspondence requests made of Walter Lippmann to speak or write, and requests for permission to reprint. That Lippmann was in great demand as a speaker appears to have been completely unnoticed by the authors of books and magazine articles about him. Yet a conservative estimate indicates that there were almost 450 such requests during this period, of which he accepted less than fifty. Except for some speeches for the Intercollegiate Socialist Society as an undergraduate and for a year or two thereafter, his earliest speech was in 1915 for the Consumers' League of New York. A year later he gave an address on American foreign policy for the City Club of New York, and in 1917 he spoke for the League of Free Nations Association on "The Fourteen Points and the League of Nations."

Lippmann usually gave one of several reasons for not accepting a request to speak. "Overwhelmed with work," or, "I only speak on political subjects," or, "I never make a speaking engagement far in advance because I never can be sure of being able to keep it," were no doubt valid reasons. But often he replied, "Making speeches is beyond my ken," or, "Lecturing is rather outside my mind," which were questionable. He did, however, accept invitations to give the Bloch Foundation lecture at Yale University in 1925, the Barbour-Page Foundation series of lectures at the University of Virginia in 1928, and several others.

Requests to speak came from learned societies, colleges and universities, City Clubs as far west as Missouri, associations, chambers of commerce, service clubs, churches, radio stations and forums. Most of the lecture bureaus, including Coit-Alber Chautauquas, Leigh-Emmerich, William B. Feakins and W. Colston Leigh approached him but never progressed beyond the talking stage.

From 1906 to 1930, Lippmann received about 200 requests to write, most of which were for articles for magazines, although there were requests for book reviews. In many cases he accepted and produced some 155 articles for thirty-seven different magazines, not including seventy signed articles for the New Republic. Also not included in the above were sixteen articles for the International magazine in 1911 and 1912, and thirty-four pieces for Vanity Fair from 1920 to 1930. Obviously, writing appealed to him more than making speeches.
In the early teens Lippmann wrote several articles as a staff member of Everybody's magazine. The editor, Lincoln Steffens, had "discovered" him at Harvard in 1910.

In 1926 and again in 1928, the Encyclopaedia Britannica approached Lippmann for articles on Joseph Pulitzer, the Monroe Doctrine, and democracy. He accepted the request for the biography of Pulitzer but refused the other two, and turned the writing of the Pulitzer piece over to Allan Nevins, who received full credit when it was published.

Requests to write were not confined to the United States. At one time or another during this period he was contacted by magazines and newspapers in London ( Observer), Japan ( Asahi), Hungary ( Pesti Maplo), India ( Aryan Path) and Russia ( Investia), among others.

Requests to reprint conclude Series II. From 1906 to 1930 there were sixty-two such requests and Lippmann granted permission in most cases, only refusing if the quotation was to be taken out of context. He usually stipulated that he see the planned use before publication as a condition of his permission.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series III is divided into Selected Correspondence, 1931-1974 and General Correspondence, 193l-l974.

Selected Correspondence is arranged alphabetically by correspondent. One folder of unidentified correspondence is filed at the end of the alphabetical listing. Also following the alphabetical listing are thirteen boxes of personal Lippmann materials (boxes 113-125). They include correspondence with Harvard University, papers concerning trips in the United States and abroad, birthday memorabilia, family correspondence, financial and legal papers, Columbia Oral History transcripts and papers of Helen Byrne Lippmann.
General Correspondence is arranged chronologically by year. Within each year, letters are grouped alphabetically. One folder of undated material has been filed at the end of the section.

The correspondence in this series begins in 1931 and contains the same format of "Selected" and "General" as Series I, which ended with the year 1930. It concludes, of course, with Walter Lippmann' s death on December 14, 1974, although some material of interest subsequent to that date is also included.

As mentioned in the introduction, the year 1931 witnessed the end of the career of Walter Lippmann as an editor, with the sale of the New York World newspaper in February 1931. His noted career as "dean of the columnists" started with his "Today and Tomorrow" column in the New York Herald Tribune in September of that year.

Lippmann continued extensive correspondence during 1931-1974 with several correspondents from the earlier period, prominent among whom were Hamilton Fish Armstrong, Newton D. Baker, Bernard Berenson, Robert H. Brand, William M. Chadbourne, Grenville Clark, Felix Frankfurter, Ralph Hayes, John Maynard Keynes, Stanley King, Thomas W. Lamont, Russell C. Leffingwell, Allan Nevins, Ellery Sedgwick and Herbert Bayard Swope. He corresponded extensively, also, with Oscar Cox and Lewis W. Douglas starting in 1932, and with Arthur W. Schlesinger, Jr., in 1950.
As the folder listing for Series III indicates, Lippmann corresponded with hundreds of other persons from all walks of life who became well known by the middle of the twentieth century and later.

Correspondence relating to Walter Lippmann's important activities as an alumnus of Harvard has been separated from other correspondence and is placed under "Harvard" at the end of the alphabetical section in boxes 113, 114 and 115. His activities included election as an Overseer in 1933 and appointment to Visiting Committees for the Departments of Government, Economics, Philosophy and the Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, as well as the Committee to Visit Harvard College.

Lippmann's relation to the Lucius W. Nieman Fellowships at Harvard "to promote and elevate standards of journalism and educate persons deemed specially qualified..." is important to note, for he was in at the creation. A member of the Board of Overseers in February 1936, when Harvard was notified of the Nieman bequest, President Conant consulted with Lippmann on the Nieman idea as early as May of that year. Lippmann joined fully with the plan and accepted appointment on the first Nieman selecting committee along with Ellery Sedgwick and John Stewart Bryan. The first fellowships, nine in number, were awarded for the academic year 1938-1939.

A release from the Harvard University News Office, dated September 15, 1977, announced a grant of $100,000.00 to the Nieman Foundation for Journalism in memory of Walter Lippmann. The grant derived from the bequest he left to Harvard at the time of his death in December 1974. The new Nieman headquarters, known as the Walter Lippmann House, will be at One Francis Avenue, a structure built in 1836 in a Greek revival style by the Harvard College carpenter, Ebenezer Francis. To match the grant and also create a full endowment for the Walter Lippmann House, a memorial fund has been launched to raise $400,000.00 from journalists and others who were friends and admirers of Lippmann.

Researchers interested in the Lippmann family papers are directed to a separate "Lippmann" section at the end of the Selected Correspondence. This section, consisting of boxes 113-123, contains all correspondence between Lippmann and Harvard University, Harvard clubs, publications and visiting committees (3 boxes). It also contains notes on more than twenty-five trips taken both in this country and abroad during the period 1934 to 1966 (3 boxes). Correspondence in other boxes in this section is concerned with Walter Lippmann's 70th, 75th, 80th and 85th birthdays, financial matters, and his several residences. The transcripts of the interviews conducted by Allan Nevins and Dean Albertson in 1953 for the Oral History Collection at Columbia University are also found here.

Correspondence between Lippmann and his second wife, Helen Byrne Armstrong, during 1937 and 1938 has been placed in box 124. This correspondence covers the period of the divorce proceedings of Walter Lippmann and his first wife, Faye (Albertson), and Helen and Hamilton Fish Armstrong; Helen's sojourn of several weeks in Reno, Nevada; and their subsequent marriage in March 1938.
Some personal correspondence and papers of Helen Byrne Lippmann were found among Walter Lippmann's papers. These have been placed in box 125 at the end of the Selected Correspondence.
Correspondence starting in 1935 which Lippmann termed "Fan Mail" is not included in Series III because of its quantity. It has been placed in its own Series V, Public Opinion Mail.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series IV is divided into the following six sections: Requests to Speak, Selected, 1931-1974; Requests to Speak, General, 1931-1974; Requests to Write, Selected, 1931-1974; Requests to Write, General, 1931-1974; Requests to Reprint, Selected, 1931-1974; Requests to Reprint, General, 1931-1974.
Selected requests are arranged alphabetically by the name of the correspondent, General requests are placed in folders by years and arranged alphabetically by correspondent within each folder.
Volume again dictated the decision to separate from his other correspondence requests made of Walter Lippmann to speak or write, and for permission to reprint during the period 1931-1974.

A conservative estimate indicates that from 1931 to 1974 there were some 3,000 requests of Lippmann to speak, of which he accepted only about 250. Notable were the Godkin Lecture at Harvard in 1934, a series of three lectures in 1938 at the University of Chicago, and again at the University of Chicago in 1939 when he gave the address on the Charles R. Walgreen Foundation. In 1945 he gave the Bergen Lecture at Yale University, the Newton D. Baker Memorial Lecture in Cleveland in 1950, the Sulgrave Manor Board Lecture in England on the Sir George Watson Chair of American History, Literature and Institutions in 1952, the Gideon D. Seymour Memorial Lecture at the University of Minnesota in 1957, and the Gaston Lecture at Georgetown University in 1963. In 1965 he addressed the International Press Institute in London and the United Nations in New York. Also of interest are his addresses at seven of the New York Herald Tribune Forums from 1932-1952.

Requests to speak came from learned societies, from more than 400 colleges and universities in this country and abroad, chambers of commerce in thirty cities from Boston to Los Angeles, radio stations in the United States, Canada and overseas, service clubs (seventeen from Rotary alone), speakers bureaus, forums and Town Halls from Maine to California. He also received requests from twenty-five groups affiliated with Harvard, and from twenty-two Phi Beta Kappa Chapters.

It was not until 1960, however, that Walter Lippmann was prevailed upon by his friend Fred W. Friendly of CBS to agree to his memorable series of six TV interviews from 1960-1964. Friendly wrote in 1964, "You are making me respectable, but I am making you rich," to which Lippmann replied, "I never suggested that there was no quid pro quo for your borrowed respectability!"

In 1943 Lippmann refused a request by Dan Golenpaul to appear on the "Information, Please" program, and again in 1968 a request to appear on the Mike Douglas Show. He also turned down an invitation from Dr. A. A. Brill to lecture at the New York Psychoanalytic Society in 1932. In a letter to Dr. Brill he wrote, "Your invitation touched my vanity in much the same way that Gene Tunney's was affected when he was invited to lecture on Shakespeare." In general, Lippmann was interested in speaking only on political subjects.

From 1931 to 1974, Lippmann received over 800 requests to write. In a good many cases he accepted, and produced over fifty articles for twenty-seven different magazines. Not included in these figures were 118 articles for Newsweek, fourteen for the Atlantic, twelve for the American magazine, eleven for Vanity Fair and eight for the Yale Review.

Requests came from encyclopedia publishers, including Americana, Britannica, Collier's, Hebraica, and Social Sciences. Book, magazine and newspaper publishers both in the United States and abroad contacted him as well, including eleven Harvard publications.

There were about 600 requests for permission to reprint during 1931-1974, and Lippmann granted most of them. These requests came from authors, book and magazine publishers, college and university publications and political parties, as well as from Grolier and other societies.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Public Opinion Mail is arranged in strictly chronological order. An attempt has been made to remove letters written by persons whose correspondence appears in Series I and III and to file it in the appropriate folder of selected correspondence.

Series V, Public Opinion Mail, is the third category of Walter Lippmann's voluminous correspondence. It was separated out in order not to clutter his important personal correspondence. Series II and IV, Requests to Speak, Write or Reprint, were created for the same reason.

In 1960, following Walter Lippmann's first TV appearance, arrangements were made to send Robert Anthony for his analysis all mail received by CBS or Lippmann in connection with the broadcast. Two hundred thirty-four letters, two hundred seven postcards and ten telegrams were received from thirty states. The analysis showed ninety-two per cent positive and eight per cent negative, probably an exceptionally high degree of agreement with the views of Lippmann on the broadcast.

Lippmann's column, "Today and Tomorrow," which began on September 8, 1931, was syndicated by the New York Herald Tribune, Inc. through December 1962, and by the Washington Post Company from 1963 to 1967 and appeared in over two hundred newspapers in this country and abroad. His public opinion mail began to arrive in great volume starting in 1935. The volume rose and fell with the interest of the readers in the particular subject which Lippmann discussed and attempted to clarify. Much of this mail was simply addressed, "Walter Lippmann, New York City," and was delivered without delay.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Magazine Articles (7 boxes) are arranged alphabetically by the name of the magazine. Articles from the same magazine are arranged chronologically. There are two boxes with forty folders containing about 175 articles which have not yet been identified. Mostly undated and without titles, they appear to be unsigned articles written for the New Republicduring the years Walter Lippmann was one of the editors.
"Today and Tomorrow" Column (14 boxes) is arranged chronologically by date of publication. Folder 232 contains several articles, most undated, which have not yet been identified as to date and title.
Other Newspaper Articles (1 box) are arranged alphabetically by newspaper. Under each newspaper, articles are arranged chronologically with undated articles at the end.
Books (12 boxes) are arranged alphabetically by title. Untitled manuscripts have been filed at the end of the section.

Addresses and Lectures (8 boxes) are arranged alphabetically by the name of the organization for which the address or lecture was given. Box 234 contains eighteen manuscripts of addresses and lectures which have not yet been identified.
Miscellaneous and Unidentified manuscripts and typescripts have been filed at the end of Series VI (box 235).
A large segment of the Walter Lippmann Papers is made up of original manuscripts and/or typescripts of his magazine and newspaper articles, his books, and his addresses and lectures.

The largest section in Series VI consists of original manuscripts of the "Today and Tomorrow" column and covers a period of about thirty-five years. An arrangement was made with Walter Lippmann many years ago for the original manuscripts of his column to be set aside for Robert Anthony's determination as to those to be preserved, and the rest burned. With very few exceptions, such as a request of a friend for the manuscript of a particular article, all manuscripts extant are here in Series VI.

It is interesting to note that Walter Lippmann never used a typewriter; rather, he wrote in longhand on plain white paper or, in later years, dictated into a machine. His writing was microscopic and rather illegible except to his secretary and a very few others who had frequent contact with it. He wrote with a large margin on the left side of the sheet, not only to leave room for changes in text but also because it gave him an indication of the length of the column. One exceptional characteristic of his writing is that so many of his manuscripts show very little in the way of revisions, even more outstanding considering the complicated subjects on which he was writing.

Manuscripts and/or typescripts of Lippmann's books make up the next largest section in this series. Altogether, eighteen of his books and several prefaces and chapters for books of others are arranged alphabetically by the title of the book. Three of his books, Drift and Mastery (1914), The Stakes of Diplomacy (1915), and Public Opinion (1921) are bound volumes of the final manuscript in Lippmann's handwriting. The partial manuscript of his last book, unfinished and tentatively entitled The Ungovernability of Man, is also found here.

Manuscripts of addresses and lectures, about 250 in number, have been arranged alphabetically by the name of the organization for which the address or lecture was given. Included are twelve Commencement addresses by Lippmann at the following institutions: Wake Forest College (1926); University of North Carolina (1927); Carnegie Institute of Technology (1928); Radcliffe College (1930); Union College (1933); University of Michigan (1934); University of Rochester (1936); Drake University (1937); Smith College (1937); Presbyterian Hospital School of Nursing (1941); University of Utah (1943); Boston University (1964).
Lippmann's addresses over radio stations CBS, NBC, WEAF and WJZ, some nineteen in number, mostly in the 1930s, are also included in this series.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series VII has two sections, Diaries (5 boxes) and Engagement Books (5 boxes). Each is arranged chronologically.
For travel notebooks, see also the papers concerning Lippmann's trips in Series III, boxes 116-118.

Unfortunately, Walter Lippmann's diaries and engagement books are not complete. Series VII contains his diaries for the years 1914-1918, 1928-1939, 1944-1972. Engagement books are for the years 1929, 1936 and 1943-1974.

Lippmann, when asked if he kept a diary, would reply, "No, not in the complete definition of a daily record of personal activities, reflections or feelings." He gave this answer to his friend, Wilmarth S. Lewis, at a luncheon at Mory's in October, 1974, when Lippmann visited the Yale Library to view an exhibition in honor of his eighty-fifth birthday, only two months before his death.
His reasons are best summed up in the first paragraph of his first diary in 1914:

"On board the S.S. Balticon July 4, 1914. Indolence and the dislike of self-consciousness have kept me from writing a diary. I dislike diaries that consist of soliloquies before the infinite. And moreover, things that happen to me and my feelings about them are not so precious that they need to be recorded in detail. Nevertheless I have regretted often that I had not set down the fresh impression of many conversations, meetings, men, things seen. The talks long ago with Prichard who opened up painting to me, my contact with William James in the last two years of his life, with Santayana, with H. G. Wells, with Graham Wallas, John Hobson, with scores of literary men, politicians, agitators here and abroad -- I should not like to lose them. I should like to be able to recall long conversations through the night with Kenneth Hunter and Felix Cole, walks over the mountains or through Britannia with Alfred Kuttuer and Lee Simonson. I should like to preserve the rich luxury of memory -- Moscow and Norway, Ireland and the Riviera -- blue and gold days by the Merrimac, long horseback rides through the Berkshires, the beach at the Lido and then again intimate understandings with Heywood and Giovannitti or with Stanley King and Kendall -- I can't put it all down."

Lippmann considered his diaries as appointment books and "not very interesting." The researcher, however, will find that this is not the case. Whenever any meeting seemed worth more than a note about the place and time, he would summarize the discussion in his tiny, cramped hand. And when he went abroad he often dictated an account of each day's events to his wife Helen. It should be pointed out to the researcher that there are several notebooks in archival boxes 116, 117, and 118 (Series III., "Lippmann, Trips") which might be considered as diaries, but which were not removed from other matters pertaining to his trips.

Included among the diaries are the notes kept by Helen at many of Lippmann's interviews with heads of state and other notables. Examples are her notebooks of Lippmann's two meetings with Khrushchev, in the fall of 1958 and the spring of 1961.

Lippmann's engagement books (Phillips Brooks appointment calendars starting in 1969) are nothing more than the usual daily notations of engagements and reminders. These entries over a period of more than thirty years, however, give an interesting view of the social and other activities of both Walter and Helen Lippmann.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series has seven sections: Degrees, Medals, Plaques, Certificates, Citations, Invitations, and Miscellaneous,
In each section, items are listed chronologically.

Lippmann's earned and honorary degrees are listed earlier in this register and include sixteen LL.D. degrees, five LITT.D. degrees and one Doctor of the University degree (York, England). He was the first American to receive the latter. His only earned degree was the A.E. cum laude from Harvard in 1910.

Medals are twenty-eight in number. Included are his first, in 1903, from Sachs Collegiate Institute, and the last, the City of New York Medallion from the hand of Mayor Abraham Beame in 1975, shortly after his eighty-fifth birthday. It was on this occasion that Lippmann saved the day in an otherwise dull affair, with his comment to the Mayor that "I hope to live long enough to deserve this."

Plaques, eight in number, are listed separately as well as a long list of certificates covering a period of over sixty years. Notable is the Presidential Medal of Freedom certificate from President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964. Also notable are certificates from several foreign countries including Belgium, France, Norway and The Netherlands.
Eleven citations, two invitations and eleven miscellaneous items complete this series.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series has four sections: Walter Lippmann Alone; Walter Lippmann With Others; Family; and Others, Miscellaneous, and Unidentified.

There are about sixty photographs, portraits, and sketches of Lippmann alone and ninety of Lippmann with others. These are arranged chronologically. Thirty family photographs and about fifty photographs of others are arranged alphabetically. Miscellaneous photographs are at the end of the series.
A folder listing for the oversize containers in this series (Oversize Box 260 and Folio 265) follows the folder titles for box 256, the last standard size archival box in Series IX.

There are about 300 photographs, portraits, and sketches in Series IX, including about 200 in which Lippmann appears. The series, therefore, has been separated into Lippmann alone, Lippmann with others, family photographs, and photographs of others including miscellaneous.

Photographs of Lippmann alone cover practically his whole long life of eighty-five years, from the age of two months (1889) to his eighty-fifth birthday party in 1974, less than three months before his death. One photograph shows him as a young lad of perhaps eight with long blond curls in his four-wheeled goat cart. Carl and Walter Binger were among his friends who also had goat carts at that time, and it is said that nobody in those days took notice of goat carts driving through the streets of New York or along Fifth Avenue, nor of the custom of driving them along the sidewalks. Another photograph shows Lippmann at his desk in the New Republic office on West 21st Street in New York City, in 1915, and as a captain in Military Intelligence in World War I.

Several fine photographs of Lippmann were taken by noted photographers of the day, including Nickolas Murray, Steichen, Fabian Bachrach, Harris and Ewing, Alfred Eisenstaedt and Henri Cartier-Bresson. Others show him at conferences and giving addresses. Altogether there are about sixty photographs, portraits, and sketches of Lippmann alone.

There are almost ninety photographs of Lippmann with others, including ambassadors, generals of World War II, statesmen and political figures here and abroad. In other fields, there are photographs with golfer Bobby Jones in the 1920s, with Clark Gable on the scene of Gone with the Wind in the 1930s, and with Douglas Fairbanks, Jr., in London.

Some thirty family photographs include two of his mother, a few of their many trips both in this country and abroad. No photographs of his father Jacob, however, have turned up in the Walter Lippmann Papers.

There are three albums in this series, with photographs of the twenty-fifth reunion of the Harvard Class of 1910; a trip to Egypt in 1934 by Lippmann and his wife Faye accompanied by Hamilton Fish Armstrong and his wife Helen, who became Lippmann's second wife in 1938; and the trip to the Suez Canal with Helen in 1959.

Also in this series are some fifty autographed or inscribed photographs from friends of Lippmann, noted personalities from Newton D. Baker to Woodrow Wilson. The series concludes with miscellaneous photographs including some of the Lippmann home, 3525 Woodley Road, N.W., Washington, D. C.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series X is the final series of the Walter Lippmann papers. The materials in Series X are arranged by type. Within each box, items are filed chronologically.

There are films of two of Walter Lippmann's television appearances on CBS News and the film shown at his memorial service in 1974, three miscellaneous recordings, twenty-six tapes including oral history tapes for the Columbia University Collection, and the dictamailer of Lippmann's final "Today and Tomorrow" column.

There are three films, two of which are CBS News 16 MM films of his first and fifth television appearances (1960 and 1963). The third is the CBS News film which was shown at the memorial service for Walter Lippmann at the Ford Foundation building in New York City on December 18, 1974. This film is a composite of the seven CBS News television appearances of Lippmann during the 1960s.

Recordings include Lippmann's pre-convention views for radio station WJZ (1936), a State Department recording for Radiodiffusion Nationale, with Lippmann speaking on the German problem in French (1947), and quotations from his book, The Communist World and Ours, produced by the League of Women Voters of the United States (1959).

Among the tapes are Lippmann's interviews for the Oral History Collection at Columbia University, an interview for the John F. Kennedy archives (1964), the tapes of Richard H. Rovere and Gary Clarkson (1964 and 1965) in connection with Rovere's start on a biography of Lippmann, and tapes of Lippmann's International Press Institute lecture in London and his United Nations address in New York in 1965.
The dictamailer is Walter Lippmann's final "Today and Tomorrow" column published on May 25, 1967.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The series is arranged alphabetically by correspondent. The correspondence predominately consists of letters written to Lippmann by various family members, friends, and business associates, with the notable exceptions of weekly letters he wrote to his parents Jacob and Daisy Lippmann during his years at Harvard and of letters he wrote to his first wife, Faye, while he was in France preparing for the Paris Peace Conference.

Letters from a number of notable individuals including Herbert Croly, Sada Cowan, Max Eastman, Felix Frankfurter, Learned Hand, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Mitchell Kennerley, Alfred Knopf, Mabel Dodge Luhan, Frances Perkins, John Reed, Theodore Roosevelt, Upton Sinclair, Lincoln Steffens, H. G. Wells, and Rebecca West supplement the original accession, but most folders only contain a few letters. There is substantial correspondence from Luhan, which discusses current events, her relationship with John Reed, and occurrences at her salon in Greenwich Village, New York City.

Several folders with topical headings are interspersed throughout the alphabetical listing, such as Fabian Society of the USA; Haywood, William; National Birth Control League, Prison reform and prisoners; and Socialist Party of New York City.

Unidentified correspondents have been placed at the end of the alphabetical listing and one folder of public opinion mail relating to Lippmann's writings can be found at the end of the listing as well.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The series is split into two sections: Harvard University and Sachs Collegiate Institute. The Harvard University files comprise the bulk of the series and are sub-divided into two headings: 1) Notebooks and 2) Papers and other writings. The Notebooks are arranged alphabetically by course name and number and consist of lecture notes kept by Lippmann for various Harvard courses. Papers and other writings are arranged by academic subject and document Lippmann's intellectual development. They often also contain grades and comments from Lippmann's professors. Two folders of Non-academic writings consist of manuscripts of articles and essays Lippmann wrote for publication while at Harvard.
The Sachs Collegiate Institute materials include Grade books, Notebooks, and Papers that document Lippmann's early school work.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Writings are arranged alphabetically under the following headings: Books; Letters to the Editor; Literary Writings; Manuscripts; Notes and Short Writings; Speeches and Interviews; and Writings of Others. Books and Manuscripts comprise the largest sections.

Arranged chronologically by publication, the Books section includes early holograph and typescript drafts, correspondence, research materials, and reviews relating to five of Lippmann's first six monographs. In particular, there is a substantial amount of material for the books A Preface to Politics and Drift and Mastery.

The Manuscripts section consists of holograph and typescript drafts of articles and essays by Lippmann, most of which were published in a variety of sources. Arranged alphabetically by title, Lippmann largely wrote these materials during the 1910s, and they cover a variety of topics such as socialism, politics, philosophy, and diplomacy, among others.

The series also includes a small number of Literary writings, which include drama, fiction, and poetry, as well as Speeches and interviews. The Writings of others section consists of manuscripts, clippings, and whole publications collected by Lippmann in the course of his own research and writing work.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The series includes diaries and engagement books, memorabilia, financial records, photographs, postcards and other materials related to Walter Lippmann, his first wife Faye Lippmann, and their families. There is a small amount of material pertaining solely to Faye Lippmann, which is listed first and includes papers relating to an art history course she took, a diary, and an engagement book. The diary has only sporadic entries and is not substantive.

The bulk of the materials are listed under the Walter Lippmann heading. There are several diaries of Lippmann, but they generally contain only cursory notes and entries are sporadic. Photographs include both prints and negatives. Most of them are candid photos that depict Walter and Faye Lippmann, other female relatives, and children vacationing at the beach. Other photographs depict unidentified adults and children at various locations, including a farm, a porch, the exterior of a residence, and on a gondola in Venice. Formal portraits of Walter Lippmann and several unidentified individuals are also included.
Two boxes of collected blank postcards from various locations in the United States and European and Latin American countries comprise the final portion of the series.
